usage: take a vehicle = 을/를 + 타다, never 에
로 marks the means of transport
the departure schedule, not the clock
examples: 기차가 와요.
The train is coming.
Simple present; 가/이 marks the subject arriving.
부산까지 기차로 세 시간 걸려요.
It takes three hours to Busan by train.
까지 = up to, 로 = by; everyday travel-time talk.
기차표를 미리 예매하지 않으면 명절에는 자리가 없어요.
If you don't book train tickets in advance, there are no seats during the holidays.
Real situation: 예매 (advance booking) is essential for 명절 travel.
nuance: 기차 (汽車, literally 'steam-vehicle') is an inter-city railway train you ride for longer trips between towns — Seoul to Busan, say — not the urban subway. The sharp dividing line learners must keep: 지하철 is the city subway/metro, 전철 is an above-ground commuter electric train, and the premium high-speed services have their own names (KTX, SRT) that Koreans use directly instead of 기차. Register is fully neutral, fine in any setting. It habitually pairs with 타다 (board), 표/기차표 (ticket), 예매하다 (book ahead), 출발하다/도착하다 (depart/arrive), and counts stations or hours of travel. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the particle on 타다: you 'get on' a train in English so people reach for 기차에 타요, but Korean treats the vehicle as a direct object — 기차를 타요. Also resist calling the subway 기차; inside a city it is almost always 지하철.

mistakes: Saying 기차에 타요 because English 'get on the train' suggests 에 — Korean uses 기차를 타다 (vehicle as object), so the correct form is 기차를 타요.
Calling the city subway 기차 — within a city Koreans say 지하철; 기차 is reserved for inter-city rail, so use 지하철을 타요 for the metro.
Saying 기차에서 가요 for going by train — to express the means you need 기차로 가요; 에서 marks where you are, not how you travel.

usage: 로 marks the means of travel
항공권 is the formal ticket word
examples: 비행기가 높이 날아요.
The airplane flies high.
Simple sentence; 날다 (to fly) is the verb that goes with it.
인천에서 비행기로 두 시간이면 도쿄에 도착해요.
From Incheon it's two hours to Tokyo by plane.
Everyday travel math: 에서 = from a starting point, 로 = by means.
비행기가 연착돼서 환승 시간을 놓칠 뻔했어요.
The flight was delayed so I almost missed my connection.
Real situation: 연착 (delay), 환승 (transfer) — airport vocabulary.
nuance: 비행기 (飛行機, literally 'fly-go-machine') is the everyday spoken word for an airplane — the aircraft you board for trips abroad or across the country. Its near-synonym 항공기 means the same machine but is a stiffer, technical/news register ('aircraft'), and the ticket has its own formal twin: spoken 비행기 표 vs. written/official 항공권. It collocates with 타다 (board), 표/항공권 (ticket), 예약하다 (reserve), 연착되다 (be delayed), 환승하다 (transfer), and 공항 (airport). As with all vehicles, the pitfall is the particle: 'get on the plane' tempts 비행기에 타요, but Korean wants the object marker — 비행기를 타요. A second subtle trap is 타다 vs 내리다: you board with 비행기를 타다 (object) but disembark with 비행기에서 내리다 (source), so the particle flips between getting on and getting off.

mistakes: Saying 비행기에 타요 to mean 'board the plane' — Korean uses the object marker, so the natural form is 비행기를 타요.
Using 비행기에서 가요 for 'go by plane' — the means takes 로, giving 비행기로 가요; 에서 only marks the place you are in.
Treating 항공권 as casual speech — in conversation Koreans usually say 비행기 표; save 항공권 for booking sites and formal writing.

examples: 자전거를 타요.
I ride a bicycle.
Core verb: 타다 covers bikes, cars, buses — anything you mount or board.
한강에서 자전거를 타면 정말 시원해요.
Riding a bike along the Han River feels really refreshing.
Everyday: 에서 marks the place of the activity; 한강 is the classic cycling spot.
따릉이를 빌려서 회사까지 자전거로 출근해요.
I rent a Ttareungi and commute to work by bike.
Real situation: 따릉이 is Seoul's public share-bike; 출근하다 = commute to work.
nuance: 자전거 (自轉車, literally 'self-turning-vehicle') is a human-powered two-wheeler for short trips or exercise, hugely popular along rivers and parks. Two near-neighbors trip learners up: its motorized cousin 오토바이 (a loanword scooter with an engine, no hanja) looks similar but is never called 자전거 since 자전거 has no motor; and 자동차 (自動車, 'self-moving-vehicle' = car) differs from 자전거 by just one hanja — 動 (move) vs 轉 (turn) — so the two written forms are easy to misread for each other. It pairs with 타다 (ride), 도로/길 (lane/path), 빌리다 (rent), 헬멧 (helmet), and brand-name share systems like 따릉이. The pitfall: English 'go by bike' and 'ride a bike' use different structures, and learners drop the right particle — for the means say 자전거로 가요 (instrumental 로), for the act of riding say 자전거를 타요 (object 를); never 자전거에 가요. Also note Koreans say 자전거를 타다, not a verb like 'pedal'.

mistakes: Saying 자전거에 가요 for 'go by bike' — the instrument particle is 로, so it must be 자전거로 가요.
Confusing 자전거 (bicycle) with 자동차 (car); they share 自...車 but differ by 轉 (turn) vs 動 (move) — keep 자전거 for the pedal bike.
Inventing a verb like 자전거해요 — Korean has no such verb; you 'ride' it with 타다, giving 자전거를 타요.

examples: 오토바이가 시끄러워요.
The motorcycle is loud.
Simple description; 시끄럽다 (noisy) is a ㅂ-irregular adjective.
배달은 보통 오토바이로 와요.
Delivery usually comes by motorcycle.
Everyday: 로 marks the means; 배달 culture runs on scooters in Korea.
오토바이는 위험하니까 헬멧을 꼭 쓰세요.
Motorcycles are dangerous, so be sure to wear a helmet.
Real situation: 위험하다 (dangerous) + 니까 (so) gives advice; 헬멧을 쓰다 = wear a helmet.
nuance: 오토바이 is a loanword adapted from English 'auto-bi(ke)' (it is NOT Sino-Korean, so there is no hanja) and names an engine-powered two-wheeler — in Korea overwhelmingly the food-delivery scooter weaving through city traffic. The crucial contrast is with 자전거: same two-wheel shape, but 오토바이 has a motor and 자전거 does not, so never swap them. A textbook word 이륜차 ('two-wheeled vehicle') exists but is officialese for signs and law; in speech everyone says 오토바이. Heavier road bikes are sometimes called 바이크. It collocates with 타다 (ride), 배달 (delivery), 헬멧 (helmet), 시끄럽다/위험하다 (loud/dangerous). The pitfall is again the vehicle particle — say 오토바이를 타요 (object), not 오토바이에 타요 — plus, because it is a foreign loanword, English speakers tend to mispronounce it; keep all four syllables o-to-ba-i, not 'motorbike'.

mistakes: Calling a 자전거 an 오토바이 — only the motorized scooter is 오토바이; the pedal bike is 자전거, so don't merge them.
Saying 오토바이에 타요 — board a vehicle with the object marker: 오토바이를 타요.
Pronouncing it like English 'motorbike' — it is the loanword 오토바이 (o-to-ba-i); using the English word will not be understood.

examples: 자동차가 많아요.
There are a lot of cars.
Simple sentence; 많다 describes quantity on the road.
주말에는 자동차로 바다에 가요.
On weekends I go to the sea by car.
Everyday: 로 = by means; a typical weekend-trip frame.
요즘은 전기 자동차를 사는 사람이 많아졌어요.
These days more people are buying electric cars.
Real situation: 전기 자동차 (EV), 많아지다 (to increase) — a current trend.
nuance: 자동차 (自動車, literally 'self-moving-vehicle') is the full, slightly formal word for a car/automobile; in everyday speech Koreans clip it to plain 차 (e.g. 차 타고 가자 'let's go by car'), so 자동차 feels more like writing, signage, or careful speech while 차 dominates conversation. Note 차 is a homonym — it also means 'tea' — but context and collocation keep them apart. It differs from 자전거 by one hanja (動 move vs 轉 turn). Habitual partners: 타다 (ride), 운전하다 (drive), 사고 (accident), 막히다 (be jammed), 전기/중고 자동차 (electric/used car). Two pitfalls: first the means particle — 자동차로 가요, not 자동차에 가요; second, 타다 means 'ride in' generally, but to say you operate the car you need a different verb, 운전하다 (drive) — don't stretch 타다 to cover driving.

mistakes: Saying 자동차에 가요 for 'go by car' — the instrumental particle is 로: 자동차로 가요.
Using 타다 to mean 'drive' — 자동차를 타다 is 'ride in a car'; to say you drive it, use 자동차를 운전하다.
Forgetting 차 alone can mean 'tea' — rely on context/collocation (차 한 잔 = a cup of tea vs 차로 가다 = go by car) so the two readings don't clash.

usage: 빨간 modifies it; the stop signal
I stop in front of the light
에서 marks the place of stopping
examples: 신호등이 빨간색이에요.
The traffic light is red.
Simple sentence; 색 names the color directly.
신호등이 초록불로 바뀌면 건너세요.
Cross when the light turns green.
Everyday: 면 (when/if) gives a condition; 초록불 = green light.
신호등을 안 지키고 건너면 정말 위험해요.
It's really dangerous to cross without obeying the lights.
Real situation: 지키다 here = obey a rule, a key collocation for signals.
nuance: 신호등 (信號燈, literally 'signal-lamp', 信號 = signal + 燈 = lamp) is the colored traffic light that controls cars and pedestrians at a crossing. Keep it apart from the bare word 신호, which means the 'signal' itself (you can 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal'), whereas 신호등 is the physical lamp unit. The individual colors get -불 ('light/fire'): 빨간불 red, 노란불 yellow, 초록불/파란불 green — and note Koreans often call the green light 파란불 ('blue light') for historical color reasons, which surprises English speakers. It collocates with 바뀌다 (change), 켜지다 (light up), 지키다 (obey), 빨간/초록 (red/green), and 건너다 (cross). The pitfall: 지키다 with 신호등 does not mean 'protect the light' as the dictionary gloss 'keep' might suggest — it means 'observe/obey' the signal, an idiom that doesn't transfer literally from English.

mistakes: Translating 신호등을 지키다 as 'protect the traffic light' — here 지키다 means 'obey/observe', so it means following the signal, not guarding it.
Confusing 신호 (the signal) with 신호등 (the lamp) — say 신호를 기다리다 'wait for the signal' but 신호등이 바뀌다 'the light changes'.
Assuming the green light is always 초록불 — Koreans commonly say 파란불 ('blue light') for go, so don't be thrown when 파란불 means green.

usage: 건너다 takes 을/를 for the thing crossed
앞 = the spot just before it
examples: 횡단보도로 건너세요.
Please cross at the crosswalk.
Simple instruction; 로 marks the route you cross by.
초록불일 때 횡단보도를 건너요.
I cross the crosswalk when the light is green.
Everyday: 일 때 (when it is) sets the timing; pairs naturally with the green light.
여기는 횡단보도가 멀어서 무단횡단하는 사람이 많아요.
The crosswalk here is far, so many people jaywalk.
Real situation: 무단횡단 = jaywalking, the opposite behavior.
nuance: 횡단보도 (橫斷步道, literally 'cross-cut-walk-path': 橫斷 = cross over + 步道 = footpath) is the striped pedestrian crossing painted on the road. Its functional opposite is 무단횡단 (無斷橫斷, 'crossing without permission' = jaywalking), and the verb that pairs with it is 건너다 (cross), not 가다. Don't confuse 횡단보도 (the painted crossing) with 인도/보도 (the sidewalk you walk along) or 육교 (the pedestrian overpass). It collocates with 건너다 (cross), 기다리다 (wait), 신호등 (the light beside it), 초록불 (green light). The pitfall is the verb-and-particle pairing of 'cross': English 'cross the street' makes learners want 길에 건너요, but 건너다 takes the object marker — 길을 건너요 / 횡단보도를 건너요 — and when you mean 'by way of the crosswalk' you switch to 횡단보도로 건너요 with instrumental 로. A four-syllable Sino-Korean word, it is easy to misspell, so lock in 횡단보도.

Mixing up 횡단보도 (crosswalk) with 인도/보도 (sidewalk) — the crosswalk spans the road; the 인도 runs alongside it.
Using 가다 instead of 건너다 — to 'cross' you need 건너다; 가다 only means 'go', so 길을 건너다 not 길을 가다 for crossing over.

usage: I park the car in the lot
I wait in the parking lot
examples: 주차장이 어디예요?
Where is the parking lot?
Simple question; 가/이 marks the subject you're locating.
지하 주차장에 차를 세웠어요.
I parked the car in the underground lot.
Everyday: 에 marks the destination of parking; 지하 = underground.
주말이라 백화점 주차장이 꽉 차서 한참 돌았어요.
It's the weekend so the department-store lot was full and I circled for ages.
Real situation: 꽉 차다 (be packed), 돌다 (circle looking for a spot).
nuance: 주차장 (駐車場, literally 'park-car-place': 駐 = stay/park + 車 = car + 場 = ground/lot) is the lot or structure where cars are parked, sometimes free, sometimes charged by the hour. Distinguish it cleanly from the verb action 주차하다 ('to park') and from the related 場 words 정거장/정류장 (a vehicle stop) — they share the 'place' character 場 but mean very different sites, and learners blur 주차장 (cars sit) with 정거장 (vehicles pause). It collocates with 세우다 (pull in/park), 주차하다 (park), 요금 (fee), 넓다/좁다 (spacious/cramped), 지하/지상 (underground/above-ground), 만차/꽉 차다 (full). The pitfall is the directional particle: because it is a destination you 'go to', use 주차장에 가요 (static goal 에), NOT 주차장에서 가요 (에서 marks where action happens or a source) — a swap English speakers make constantly. Also park a car with 세우다 or 주차하다, not 만들다.

Distinguish it cleanly from the verb action 주차하다 ('to park') and from the related 場 words 정거장/정류장 (a vehicle stop) — they share the 'place' character 場 but mean very different sites, and learners blur 주차장 (cars sit) with 정거장 (vehicles pause).
駐車場, literally 'park-car-place': 駐 = stay/park + 車 = car + 場 = ground/lot.

The pitfall is the directional particle: because it is a destination you 'go to', use 주차장에 가요 (static goal 에), NOT 주차장에서 가요 (에서 marks where action happens or a source) — a swap English speakers make constantly. Also park a car with 세우다 or 주차하다, not 만들다.

mistakes: Writing 주차장에서 가요 to mean 'go to the parking lot' — going to a destination takes 에, so it's 주차장에 가요; 에서 marks where you do something or move out from.
Confusing 주차장 (where cars are parked) with 정거장 (where a bus/train stops) — both end in 場, but one is for parked cars, the other for boarding.
Saying 차를 주차장에 만들어요 for parking — to park you use 세우다 or 주차하다: 차를 주차장에 세워요.

usage: 넣다 = put in / fill up the tank
written solid; the cost of fuel
떨어지다 = run out / be used up
the proper word for kitchen oil
examples: 기름이 없어요.
There's no gas / oil.
Simple existence sentence with 가/이 + 없다.
주유소에서 기름을 가득 넣었어요.
I filled up the tank at the gas station.
Everyday: 가득 = full; 주유소 = gas station, the place you 넣다 fuel.
요즘 기름값이 너무 올라서 차를 잘 안 타게 돼요.
Fuel prices have risen so much lately that I barely drive.
Real situation: 기름값 (fuel price) + 오르다 (rise); a common complaint.
nuance: 기름 is a native Korean word (no hanja) covering both car fuel and cooking/edible oil, so context decides whether it means gasoline or kitchen oil. The precise dividing lines: the formal/technical fuel word is 연료 (燃料, 'burn-material' = fuel in general) and the pump itself is 휘발유 (gasoline) or 경유 (diesel), while kitchen oil is properly 식용유 ('edible oil') or named by source (참기름 sesame oil, 올리브유 olive oil). So 기름 is the casual umbrella term; specialists narrow it down. It collocates with 넣다 (fill up), 값 (price → 기름값), 떨어지다 (run out), 가득 (full tank), 주유소 (gas station). The pitfall: don't say 기름을 채우다 by analogy with English 'fill up'; the idiomatic verb is 넣다 ('put in') — 기름을 넣다. And when you mean engine fuel specifically in formal contexts, English speakers reach for a loanword like 가솔린, but everyday Korean just says 기름.

mistakes: Assuming 기름 only means car gasoline — it equally means cooking oil, so for the kitchen specify 식용유/참기름 to avoid 'I put gasoline in the pan'.
Saying 기름을 채워요 for 'fill up' — the natural verb is 넣다: 기름을 넣어요 (or 가득 넣다 to fill the tank).
Using a loanword like 가솔린 in casual speech — Koreans say 기름 for fuel at the pump; 가솔린/휘발유 sound technical or like a label.

examples: 요금이 얼마예요?
How much is the fare?
Simple price question with 가/이 + 얼마.
버스 요금을 교통카드로 냈어요.
I paid the bus fare with a transit card.
Everyday: 로 marks the means of payment; 내다 = pay.
택시 요금이 기본요금보다 훨씬 많이 나왔어요.
The taxi fare came out much higher than the base fare.
Real situation: 기본요금 (base fare), 나오다 (be tallied) — how charges 'come out'.
nuance: 요금 (料金, literally 'charge-money': 料 = fee/materials + 金 = money) is the set, rate-based charge for using a service — a ride, phone line, utility, or hotel — fixed by a published tariff. Contrast it sharply with 값/가격 (the price of a physical thing you buy) and with 비용 (the broader 'cost/expense' you incur): you pay 요금 for a bus ride but 값/가격 for a bag, and you calculate total 비용 for a trip. Within transit it pairs as 버스/택시/지하철 요금 (fare), 기본요금 (base fare), 요금을 내다 (pay), 오르다/인상되다 (rise), 할인 (discount). The pitfall: English 'price' makes learners say 기차 값 for a fare, but a service charge is 요금 (기차 요금), and a ticket's price is 표 값 / 표 가격 — so the fare to ride and the price of the ticket are worded differently. Pay it with 내다, not 사다 (you don't 'buy' a fare).

Confusing 요금 with 비용 — 요금 is the fixed rate for one service, while 비용 is overall cost/expense, so a whole trip's spending is 여행 비용, not 여행 요금.

usage: I get off at the stop
the upcoming one on the route
examples: 다음 정거장에서 내려요.
I get off at the next stop.
Everyday: 에서 + 내리다 is the fixed pattern for getting off.
우리 집은 여기서 세 정거장이에요.
My place is three stops from here.
Counting stops as a distance measure — a very common usage.
버스 정거장이 이사하면서 위치가 바뀌었어요.
The bus stop's location changed when it was moved.
Real situation: 정거장 as a fixed point whose 위치 (location) can change.
nuance: 정거장 (停車場, literally 'stop-car-place': 停 = halt + 車 = vehicle + 場 = ground) is a stop where a vehicle pauses to let people on and off, and it doubles as a counting unit ('two stops away'). The near-synonyms split by formality and mode: 정류장 (停留場) is the standard modern word for a bus stop (버스정류장), 정거장 sounds slightly older/literary and is also used loosely for stations, while a big rail/subway terminal is a 역 (驛, 'station'). So for a bus today most Koreans say 정류장; 역 is for trains/subway lines. It collocates with 내리다 (get off), 다음/이번 (next/this), 버스 (bus), counting 한/두/세 정거장. Two pitfalls: getting off uses 에서 + 내리다 (not 를), and English speakers blur the 場-words — keep 정거장/정류장 (a pause-and-board point) apart from 주차장 (a place cars are parked) and from 역 (a rail station building).

Confusing 정거장/정류장 (a stop) with 역 (a station) — use 역 for subway/train terminals (서울역) and 정류장 for a bus stop.
Mixing up 정거장 with 주차장 — both end in 場 but 정거장 is where a vehicle pauses to board, 주차장 is where cars are parked; don't swap them.

examples: 교통이 복잡해요.
The traffic is heavy.
Simple description; 복잡하다 is the go-to word for congestion.
서울은 대중교통이 정말 편리해요.
Public transit is really convenient in Seoul.
Everyday: 대중교통 names the whole bus-and-subway system as a subject.
출퇴근 시간에는 교통 체증이 심해서 지하철이 더 빨라요.
During rush hour the traffic jam is bad, so the subway is faster.
Real situation: 교통 체증 (traffic jam), 출퇴근 (commute) — comparing modes.
nuance: 교통 (交通, literally 'exchange-pass': 交 = cross/exchange + 通 = go through/communicate) is the broad abstract noun for the movement and flow of vehicles and people — the whole system of getting around, plus 'traffic' as in congestion. It is NOT a countable single vehicle: that is the pitfall — English 'a lot of traffic' is fine, but you can't use 교통 for 'a car' or 'a bus'; for those say 차/버스. Distinguish 교통 (the system/flow) from 교통수단 (交通手段, 'means of transport' = the specific modes) and from 길/도로 (the road itself). High-frequency compounds: 대중교통 (public transit), 교통카드 (transit card), 교통사고 (accident), 교통 체증/혼잡 (congestion), 교통편 (transport connection). When traffic is bad, Koreans say 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다 ('the road is blocked'); when it flows, 교통이 원활하다. Don't say 교통이 많다 for 'heavy traffic' — the natural adjective is 복잡하다 or 막히다.

mistakes: Using 교통 for a single vehicle — it means transit/traffic as a whole, not 'a car'; for one vehicle say 차, 버스, etc.
Saying 교통이 많아요 for 'heavy traffic' — the idiomatic phrasing is 교통이 복잡하다 or 길이 막히다; 많다 doesn't collocate here.
Confusing 교통 with 교통수단 — 교통 is the overall flow/system, while 교통수단 is the specific means (bus, subway, car), so 'which transport do you take?' is 무슨 교통수단, not 무슨 교통.
